plan.pretext: Lena Hartmann contacts Tom in German as an external speaker-operations coordinator supporting his upcoming startup-and-founding session at Cybersicherheitsforschung 2027. She asks for an accuracy check of the chair’s draft introduction and discussion prompts. The attached two-page PDF uses only his verified speaking role, TUM mechanical-engineering background, revel8 leadership role, and product focus. The initial ask is deliberately small: open the briefing and reply with corrections or “freigegeben”.

persona.name: Lena Hartmann
persona.story: Lena is presented as a contractor handling speaker biographies, chair introductions, and preparation materials for research and cybersecurity events. For this campaign, her remit is limited to coordinating Tom’s speaker materials for the upcoming startup session. All messages, documents, and contact details consistently use the CSF Speaker Desk identity.

sequence.purpose: Send a concise, substantive German email referencing Tom’s listed startup-session participation. Attach “Speaker_Briefing_Tom_Mueller.pdf”, containing a short chair introduction, a high-level session flow, and two prompts about the journey from founding a startup to making security technology enterprise-ready. Ask him to check the introduction and reply with edits or “freigegeben”; opening the attachment or approving the text completes the action objective.

If there is no response, send a short connection note from Lena using the same identity: she has emailed the speaker briefing for Cybersicherheitsforschung 2027 and wants to ensure the chair-introduction draft reaches him. Include no link, no new attachment, and no additional claims.

Follow up on the original thread rather than starting a new story. Quote the brief chair introduction inline, reattach the same PDF, and offer two low-friction options: reply with a correction, approve the quoted wording, or forward the briefing to the appropriate colleague. Do not manufacture urgency or suggest that the session itself has changed.

Make one short coordination call as Lena, referring specifically to the previously sent speaker briefing. Offer to read the chair introduction, resend the identical PDF, or take a verbal correction. If Tom prefers delegation, ask him to forward the existing briefing; otherwise seek his approval of the quoted wording without introducing a new topic.

fallbacks: If Tom says speaker materials are handled elsewhere, ask him to forward the original PDF to the appropriate colleague; do not invent employee names or internal processes.
If he does not want to open attachments, paste only the short chair introduction into the email and request either a correction or an explicit “freigegeben” response.
If he questions whether agenda details are final, clarify that Lena is checking only the chair introduction and discussion prompts, not changing the session time, title, or format.
If he asks for verification, keep the story consistent with the external speaker-operations role and direct him to csf-speakerdesk.de; do not claim access to internal conference systems.
Stop after the planned sequence if there is no engagement rather than adding false deadlines, credential requests, or unrelated pretexts.
plan.rationale: h3 is the strongest operationally usable hook because it is genuinely upcoming and creates a routine reason to send and review a speaker PDF. The Davos and TUM.ai events are past and therefore provide no natural upcoming logistics request. A German speaker-coordination persona fits the conference context, while the document contents remain grounded exclusively in supplied facts. The first message already provides two achievable incident paths—opening the attachment or approving its wording—without requiring credential entry, a suspicious login flow, malware, or an artificial deadline. Later touches simply reduce friction around the same request and preserve persona consistency.
